Part I Writing (30 minutes)
Directions: Suppose the student union of your university is collecting opinions on improving its work for the coming year. You are now to write a response by suggesting how it can better enrich student life. You will have 30 minutes to write the essay. You should write at least 120 words but no more than 180 words.
Part II Listening Comprehension (25 minutes)

People tend to want as many choices as possible. They believe this will maximize their __26__ of making the best decision. Some research shows that, when it comes to actually making a __27__ from all of these choices, people can become __28__ and avoid making a decision altogether. Even worse, when people finally do decide, they may be less satisfied with their decision and feel more regretful over whatever choice they made.
Why does this happen? Some studies suggest that, under demanding conditions, people choosing from many options may __29__ more effort in the decision yet feel less confident. The effect depends on factors such as task complexity and how clear their preferences are. In other words, when we are __30__ with more choices, making the “right” or “correct” decision begins to feel more __31__ and, at the same time, more difficult to do. This may contribute to the deep fear that we will make the wrong decision.
How can we solve this problem? I believe this fear could be tempered by putting decisions into perspective. It might help to remember that many of the choices you make, such as what to have for lunch, will not __32__ much in the future and that, even more important choices, like accepting a new job, can sometimes __33__ be changed, though changing them may involve costs. It could also help to __34__ these situations with clear guidelines and ideas of what you want from the __35__ of options, which can narrow the possible choices, and also make you more confident about your ability to make the right decision.

Section B

阅读说明：本文改编自 2023 年评论；Skillman 数据来自 2022 年调查，比较 2017 年春与 2019–2020 年冬的季度总销售，不能证明自行车道的独立因果效应。综述是 23 项研究，不是 23 座城市；任期、时间和对应题干已校正。
The battle over bike lanes needs a mindset shift
A) In 2017, New York City announced that it would be putting bike lanes onto a stretch of Skillman Ave in Queens — and removing 116 parking spots. Cyclists loved the plan, but local business owners got very angry. Taking out those parking spots, as they argued at protests and in letters to the city council, would ruin stores and restaurants along Skillman. “Parking here is already a nightmare,” one shouted at a protest rally.
B) But the bike lanes were a done deal, and soon they were in place. In a September 2022 investigation, Jesse Coburn — an investigative writer with Streetsblog New York — wondered whether those predictions of economic collapse came true. So he asked the city’s Department of Finance to give him a few years’ worth of sales figures for that stretch of Skillman Ave. How had the businesses on that street fared?
C) Quite well, it turns out. Comparing spring 2017 with winter 2019–2020, his analysis found a 12 percent rise in aggregate quarterly taxable sales along the studied stretch of Skillman, compared with 3 percent in Queens overall. The lane was installed in autumn 2018. The stretch also gained three businesses, while Queens had a net loss. These aggregate figures do not establish that the lane caused the increase or that every shop benefited.
D) The thing is, the actual merchants along Skillman? They didn’t believe it. When Coburn spoke to them and described what he’d found, only a few store owners admitted the lanes had helped. Many still insisted the lanes were killing their part of the city. And emotions ran hot: Someone scattered tacks (大头钉) on the bike lane.
E) This little story turns out to be a fascinating glimpse at the challenges cities face as they try to update their urban infrastructure — to clean up the air, reduce greenhouse emissions, and speed up travel by making towns more bike-friendly. A growing body of research suggests that bike lanes and pedestrian improvements can support local commerce. Benefits vary by place and business, and removing parking does not guarantee higher sales. But the folks who run local businesses simply aren’t convinced, even when their own street performs. Given that sort of mess, can political fights over bike lanes ever end?
F) In 2013, New York City’s Department of Transportation reported seven case studies of street improvements, including bicycle lanes, pedestrian spaces and bus-service projects. Several project areas showed retail sales growth that exceeded nearby or borough-wide trends. The comparison supports the economic case for well-designed streets, but it is not a guarantee for every shop or proof that every effect came from cycling alone.
G) Beyond New York, a 2021 review of 23 studies generally found positive or statistically non-significant effects on nearby retail and food-service businesses. It also noted possible negative effects on car-oriented businesses and limitations in the available evidence.
H) The truth is that in fairly dense areas, bikes are more efficient at moving people around. You might lose one car driver’s business — but you may gain shoppers who can arrive more easily on bikes. “Cyclists and pedestrians are consumers too,” notes Professor Susan Handy. Plus, streets redesigned for bikes and pedestrians tend to become more pleasant places to hang around, so “in a lot of cases, that’s created much nicer environments that are really good for those businesses.”
I) Mom-and-pop shops are usually pretty quick at recognizing situations that will help their bottom lines. So why the blind spot here? Perhaps it’s that attention focuses on horror stories — and some merchants do get hit when bike lanes come in.
J) I spoke to Cindy Hughes, a hairdresser (理发师) in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She said business fell by at least 40 percent when the city removed nearby parking to put in a bike lane. The majority of her customers drive, with many coming from nearby towns. Only a very few have shifted to cycling, and she doubted that even those customers would cycle in Boston’s snowy winters. So while Hughes supports bike lanes — “cyclists deserve to be safe” — she sees the parking loss as an existential risk. “Look, 90 percent of my customers drive,” she told me. “For our business, the bike lanes are way worse than Covid was.”
K) For others, the pushback is cultural, says Henry Grabar, a writer for the Slate Magazine. Small business owners are frequently drivers who commute from other parts of the city by car, Grabar points out. They're also often longtime locals. “They tend to be people with deep roots in the city, who have hung around since before the neighborhood became what it is today,” he adds. Driving around town in a car is so normal to them that cycling seems weird and unusual — despite the increased popularity of cycling during the pandemic described in the original article.
L) Psychology beats all! Who knew, right? The fierce divide between store owners and bike-lane advocates seems similar to our larger culture wars over climate change. In my view, data alone may do little to change minds in such disputes.
M) When Janette Sadik-Khan was the head of New York City’s Transportation Department after her appointment in 2007, she oversaw a rollout (推出) of bike lanes — and got angry blowback from residents and business owners who claimed there weren’t enough cyclists to justify installing lanes. In the original 2023 article, she noted ironically that the lanes had become so busy that opponents were making the opposite complaint: too many cyclists were getting in the way of cars.
N) Maybe bike lanes will always be charged with emotion, until enough of the public is finally concerned about climate change — and it seems reckless (鲁莽的) to not have them.
O) Crises, after all, have a way of opening people’s eyes to possibilities. During Covid, restaurants and cafes lost so much business that cities nationwide began allowing them to build curbside seating areas where people could sit in the open air. This reduced parking, but the crisis made some shop owners more willing to accept the change. By the time of the original article, some cities were considering or adopting lasting outdoor-dining arrangements. A 2022 New York City study of five Open Streets corridors found favorable restaurant and bar sales patterns relative to comparison areas, although results varied by corridor. If data won’t change minds, customers might.

Passage One
Questions 46 to 50 are based on the following passage.
研究说明：本文改编自 Tobias Eckle 的 2022 年文章。1969 年研究的是大鼠肝酶节律，不是辛伐他汀临床试验；午夜咪达唑仑结果为观察关联，整体样本未见关联。用药应遵循具体处方，不能自行按文章调整。第 50 题限定问研究需要，以消除原 A/C 两项重叠。
Many organisms have internal daily rhythms that are synchronized by environmental cues, including the day-night cycle. Human sleep and many other body functions follow roughly 24-hour rhythms, and the timing of behaviors like exercise or food intake can significantly influence your health. For example, late eating may affect metabolism and weight, but its effects also depend on total intake, sleep, activity and individual circumstances.
Many drug targets in the body follow a 24-hour cycle, too. This means that the specific proteins a drug is designed to modify can react differently to the medicine over the course of a 24-hour time period. Because how the body responds to a drug can differ depending on the time it is taken, it logically follows that taking medicines at specific times could help increase their effectiveness and reduce unwanted side effects.
In this 2022 article, the author argues that time-of-day effects receive too little attention in prescribing. He identifies limited awareness and incomplete research as barriers. For medicines without a demonstrated time-specific advantage, a consistent morning or evening routine may be chosen to help patients take them as instructed. Some medicines already have specific timing instructions, which patients should follow.
Research on daily rhythms in a liver enzyme (酶) involved in cholesterol production dates back to 1969, but that work studied rats, not simvastatin treatment in patients. Simvastatin was first approved in the US in 1991. Its prescribing information recommends evening dosing; this drug-specific recommendation should not be generalized to all medicines.
Timing may also affect adverse outcomes. My colleagues and I studied midazolam, a widely used sedative (镇静剂), in surgical records from 50 institutions for 2014–2019. We found no association with myocardial injury across the full study population, but an association in overnight surgery. This observational finding does not prove causation or establish a universal safe or unsafe administration time; it calls for further clinical investigation.
More research is needed to determine the best times to administer treatments for different diseases. I believe taking drug timing into account could help make treatments more effective and help more people worldwide.

A) It has a considerable impact on our health.
B) It confines us to a 24-hour day-night cycle.
C) It requires us to follow a particular rhythm.
D) It holds the key to all human body functions.
47. What does the author say about some proteins targeted by drugs?
A) They can modify the effects of medicines in different ways.
B) They can reduce unwanted side effects of certain medicines.
C) Their reaction to medicines can vary during the day-night cycle.
D) Their design determines how differently they react to medicines.
48. What concern does the author express about doctors’ prescribing practices?
A) Time-of-day effects may receive too little consideration.
B) They rarely consider which medicine works better for which patient.
C) They tell patients its possible side effects during a period of 24 hours.
D) They tell patients to comply with the directions of drug manufacturers.
49. Why may a consistent morning or evening routine be chosen when no time-specific advantage has been established?
A) To discourage them from making complaints.
B) To ensure they take the drugs as instructed.
C) To comply with new research findings strictly.
D) To guarantee the maximum effect of the drugs.
50. What research need does the author identify in the final paragraph?
A) Considering drug-taking timing when prescribing drugs for patients.
B) Making treatments less complex by taking drug timing into account.
C) Conducting more studies to find out the best timing for treating different diseases.
D) Finding out the most effective drugs for treating diseases through further research.
Passage Two
Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：就业比例反映原报道引用的 2018 年前后历史数据；学历分组相关性不证明学历直接导致延迟退休，Baily 对动机的说明是其解释。第 52 题限定问工资，第 53 题明确数据年份与分组含义。
Katharine Abraham, an economics professor, was chatting with her hairdresser (理发师) about retirement plans. The economist said she plans to continue working because she wants to. The hairdresser agreed but for a different reason: She needs the money.
Both scenarios (情况) were cited in the original report as reasons for increased employment among Americans in their 70s. Looking back over roughly two decades to 2018, the article reported a rise in the share working from under 10% to nearly 15%. These are historical figures, not the current rate.
In addition to people being healthier and living much longer, economists say that a combination of financial considerations such as years of slow rise in real wages and a shift away from traditional pensions in the private sector are some of the reasons people delay retirement. The decline of manufacturing and the increase in the number of people working in less labor-intensive occupations also have contributed to the trend, says Abraham, who researches work and retirement decisions of older Americans.
“Which matters more depends on what your history up until that point has been in the type of work you’re doing,” Abraham says.
The article reported increases across education groups, although the percentages vary by category. The share of Americans with bachelor's degrees who were working into their 70s reached nearly 20% in 2018. For those with a high school degree or less, the corresponding 2018 proportion had risen to around 10%, while those with some college education were in the middle at around 15%.
Martin Neil Baily, an economist described in the original report as leading a research project on retirement security, notes that quitting a career can lead to feelings of isolation and loneliness, particularly for men. He suggests that many college-educated workers are choosing to stay in the labor force more for social benefits than for financial reasons. They’re also more likely to be in professional occupations where they tend to enjoy their work more.
Workers in more physical jobs, meanwhile, may be more likely to look forward to retiring, Baily says, suggesting those who stay on are more likely doing so for financial reasons.
51. What do we learn from the passage about the economics professor and her hairdresser?
A) They differ in their reasons for continuing to work.
B) They are both committed to working into their 70s.
C) They are happy about their current financial situation.
D) They hold different views about postponing retirement.
52. What wage-related reason does the passage give for delayed retirement?
A) More and more people have switched to less intellectually challenging jobs.
B) The number of jobs suitable for older people has increased in the private sector.
C) Wages in terms of purchasing power had grown slowly for years.
D) More and more people in the workplace find it hard to rely on traditional pensions.
53. What pattern across education groups does the article report for people in their 70s in 2018?
A) The higher their earnings, the more likely they are tempted to delay retirement.
B) Those who have more job satisfaction tend to retire later than those who have less.
C) More men than women are likely to stay in the labor force until their late seventies.
D) The share working was higher in groups with more education.
54. What motive does Baily suggest is especially important for many college-educated workers who keep working?
A) Enjoying financial security.
B) Staying connected socially.
C) Contributing more professionally.
D) Increasing social security payments.
55. What does the passage say about people doing manual work?
A) They are eager to enjoy life after retiring.
B) They are likely to have financial troubles.
C) They generally don't enjoy doing it.
D) They tend to anticipate retirement.
